solution: In H\(_2\)SO\(_4\), S has 2 single S-OH bonds and 2 double S=O bonds; \(2 \times 1 + 2 \times 2 = 6\) shared pairs, and \(6 \times 2 = 12\) electrons around S (no lone pairs). Matches option D.
note: 4 bonds (8 e) + lone pairs = 12 does not add up; S has 6 shared pairs (2 single + 2 double) = 12 electrons, no lone pairs

solution: In IF, iodine has 3 lone pairs (7 valence electrons, 1 used for bond) and fluorine has 3 lone pairs. The question counts the lone pairs on the central atom I, which is 3 (the 3 on F are not counted). Matches option A: 3.
note: sentence 1 computed 6 for the stem then jumped to 3; the paper's key table counts the lone pairs on the central halogen (3)

solution: Rate \(= \frac{1}{2}\frac{d[\text{SO}_4^{2-}]}{dt} = -\frac{d[\text{S}_2\text{O}_8^{2-}]}{dt}\) (both have stoichiometry ratio 1:2). So the rate of disappearance \(-\frac{d[\text{S}_2\text{O}_8^{2-}]}{dt} = \frac{1}{2} \times 2.2\times10^{-2} = 1.1\times10^{-2}\). Matches option A.
note: lost minus on the reactant S2O8(2-): rate = -d[S2O8]/dt, so the 1.1e-2 is its rate of disappearance (the paper's stem and key print the unsigned d[S2O8]/dt)

solution: Rate \(= -\frac{1}{3}\frac{d[\text{I}^-]}{dt} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{d[\text{SO}_4^{2-}]}{dt}\). Rate of I\(^-\) consumption \(= \frac{3}{2} \times 0.044 = 0.066\). Matches option C.
note: lost minus on the consumed I-: rate = -1/3 d[I-]/dt (paper's own key has it)

solution: Rate relation: \(-\frac{1}{2}\frac{d[\text{N}_2\text{O}_5]}{dt} = \frac{d[\text{O}_2]}{dt}\). Reading the stem's 0.02 as the rate of disappearance \(-\frac{d[\text{N}_2\text{O}_5]}{dt}\), \(\frac{d[\text{O}_2]}{dt} = 0.02/2 = 0.01\) mol dm\(^{-3}\) s\(^{-1}\). Matches option A: 0.01 mol dm\(^{-3}\) s\(^{-1}\).
note: stem prints d[N2O5]/dt = +0.02 (the paper drops the sign; its own solution has +1/2 d[N2O5]/dt = d[O2]/dt); with the minus in line 0 the 0.02 must be read as the rate of disappearance

solution: In \(\text{Fe(CN)}_6^{4-}\): overall charge = -4. Six CN\(^-\) contribute \(6 \times (-1) = -6\). So Fe + (-6) = -4, giving Fe = +2. Matches option A: +2.
note: one CN- contributes -1, six contribute -6

solution: \([\text{OH}^-]=0.001\times0.02=2\times10^{-5}\,\text{M}\). Undissociated base \(=0.001\times0.98=9.8\times10^{-4}\,\text{M}\). \(K_b=\dfrac{(2\times10^{-5})^2}{9.8\times10^{-4}}\approx4\times10^{-7}\). Matches option A: \(4\times10^{-7}\).

Edge \(a = 336\,\text{pm} = 3.36\times10^{-8}\,\text{cm}\); \(V_{cell} = a^3 = 3.79\times10^{-23}\,\text{cm}^3\). Mass of one simple-cubic cell (1 atom) \(= \rho V = 9.4\times3.79\times10^{-23} = 3.56\times10^{-22}\,\text{g}\). Number of atoms in 5 g \(= \dfrac{5}{3.56\times10^{-22}} \approx 1.4\times10^{22}\). Matches option C: \(1.4\times10^{22}\).
Moles of solute \(= 46/46 = 1\); moles of water \(= 162/18 = 9\). \(\Delta P/P_0 \approx n_2/n_1 = 1/9 = 0.11\). Matches option C: 0.11.
note: 0.1 does not round to 0.11. The paper keys C with the dilute form dP/P0 = W2M1/(M2W1) = (46x18)/(46x162) = 0.11 (its own AK line); stored text now follows that. Exact n2/(n1+n2) is 0.1, which is not an option.

solution: Molality \(m=\dfrac{4/126}{0.080\,\text{kg}}=\dfrac{0.03175}{0.080}=0.397\,\text{mol kg}^{-1}\). \(\Delta T_f=K_f\cdot m=1.86\times0.397=0.74\,\text{K}\). Matches option B: 0.74 K.
Molarity \(C=\frac{1.7/111}{1.25}=\frac{0.015315}{1.25}=0.012252\,M\). \(\pi=iCRT=2.47\times0.012252\times0.082\times300\approx0.744\,\text{atm}\). Matches option B.
Mass of 1 atom \(=10\,u\times1.66056\times10^{-24}\,g/u=1.66056\times10^{-23}\,g\). Matches option B.
note: 10 g/mol / 6.022e23 is 1.66e-24 g (one u), not 1.66e-23 g; an atom of 10 u weighs 10 x 1.66056e-24 g. Paper's key B agrees with the fixed text.

solution: \(2KClO_3 \rightarrow 2KCl + 3O_2\); 1 mol \(O_2\) requires \(2/3\) mol \(KClO_3 = \frac{2}{3} \times 122.5 = 81.67\) g. Matches option B: 81.67 g.

Ethanol is \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}\), i.e. \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_6\text{O}\).
Molar mass \(= 2(12.011) + 6(1.008) + 15.999 = 46.069\,\text{g}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\).
One mole carries one oxygen atom, of mass \(15.999\,\text{g}\).
Mass per cent of oxygen \(= \dfrac{15.999}{46.069} \times 100 = 34.73\%\).
Matches option D.
note: 16/46 x 100 = 34.78, not 34.73; 34.73 needs the exact masses 15.999/46.069, so the working uses them throughout

solution:
Glucose \(C_{6}H_{12}O_{6}\) has 6 carbon atoms per molecule.
Carbon atoms \(= 0.35 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} \times 6 = 1.2646 \times 10^{24}\) (option C prints \(1.264 \times 10^{24}\)).
note: 0.35 x 6.022 x 6 = 12.6462, so 1.2646e24 (the paper's own key solution says 1.2646e24); option C prints the truncated 1.264e24

solution:
Take \(1\,\text{L}\) of solution.
Mass of solution \(= 1000 \times 1.025 = 1025\,\text{g}\).
It holds \(2\,\text{mol}\) of ethanol, mass \(= 2 \times 46 = 92\,\text{g}\).
Mass of water \(= 1025 - 92 = 933\,\text{g} = 0.933\,\text{kg}\).
Molality \(= \dfrac{2}{0.933} = 2.1436\,\text{m}\) (option B prints \(2.143\)).
Matches option B.
note: 2/0.933 = 2.1436; option B prints it truncated as 2.143

solution: Molar mass of H₂O = 18 g mol⁻¹. \(n = 91.0\text{ g}/18\text{ g mol}^{-1} \approx 5.06\) mol, so the nearest option is \(5.0\). Matches option D.
note: 91.0/18 = 5.0556 = 5.06, which rounds to 5.1 not 5.0 (the paper's own key solution writes 5.05 ~ 5.0); option D is the nearest

solution: Energy of one photon \(E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{(6.626\times 10^{-34})(3\times 10^{8})}{700\times 10^{-9}} = 2.840\times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}\). Per mole \(= 2.840\times 10^{-19} \times 6.022\times 10^{23} = 1.71\times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{J}\).
note: hc/lambda = 2.8397e-19 rounds to 2.840e-19, not 2.839e-19; per mole still 1.71e5 J (key A)

Angular momentum \(mvr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}\); for the first orbit n = 1.
\(= \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34}}{2\pi} = 1.05 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{kg m}^2\text{s}^{-1}\).
note: 6.626e-34/(2 x 3.14) = 1.0551e-34 rounds to 1.06; with 2 pi it is 1.0546e-34 = 1.05 (key A). The paper's own key solution prints 2 x 3.14 = 1.05

solution: Magnetic moment \(\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\) BM. Mn\(^{2+}\): [Ar]3d\(^5\), 5 unpaired electrons, \(\mu = \sqrt{35} = 5.92\) BM, the highest. Fe\(^{2+}\): 4 unpaired (4.90 BM), Cr\(^{2+}\): 4 unpaired (4.90 BM), Ni\(^{2+}\): 2 unpaired (2.83 BM). Matches option C: Mn.

Intersections: \((x-1)^2=\tfrac{1}{4}\Rightarrow x=\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{3}{2}\); \((x+1)^2=\tfrac{1}{4}\Rightarrow x=-\tfrac{3}{2},-\tfrac{1}{2}\). By symmetry, area \(=2\int_0^{1/2}\left[(x-1)^2-\tfrac{1}{4}\right]dx=2\left[\dfrac{(x-1)^3}{3}-\dfrac{x}{4}\right]_0^{1/2}=\tfrac{1}{3}\). Matches option A: \(\tfrac{1}{3}\) sq. units.
note: integrand sign was reversed (negative on [0,1/2]); the '...' hid the evaluation, now written out. Paper key (a) = 1/3 agrees

solution: Intersection points: \(y = -2, 4\) (i.e., \(x = 1, 4\)). Area \(= \int_{-2}^{4}\left[\frac{y+4}{2} - \frac{y^2}{4}\right]dy = 9\) sq. units. Matches option D: 9 sq. units.
note: integrand sign reversed: the line x=(y+4)/2 is on the right, so the integral printed gives -9
lower limit of [x ln x - x] is -1, so subtracting it gives -(-1) inside the bracket, i.e. -(2 ln2 - 2) - 1, not +1; result e^2-e+1-2ln2 (key C) unchanged

solution: The region is inside the unit circle AND left of the parabola \(x = 1-y^2\). Left of the \(y\)-axis the region is a half disc of area \(\frac{1}{2}\pi\cdot1^2=\frac{\pi}{2}\); right of it, between the \(y\)-axis and the parabola, the area is \(2\int_0^1(1-y^2)\,dy=2\left[y-\dfrac{y^3}{3}\right]_0^1=\dfrac{4}{3}\). The result is \(\frac{\pi}{2} + \frac{4}{3}\). Common mistake: incorrect setup of limits of integration for the two bounding curves.
note: working was only a description; written out. x^2+y^2<=1 and x<=1-y^2: left half disc pi/2 plus 2*int_0^1(1-y^2)dy = 4/3; key B

solution: The total \(\sum_{r=0}^{n}\frac{\binom{n}{r}}{32}=1\Rightarrow\frac{2^n}{32}=1\Rightarrow 2^n=32=2^5\Rightarrow n=5\). \(P(X\leq2)=\frac{\binom{5}{0}+\binom{5}{1}+\binom{5}{2}}{32}=\frac{16}{32}=\frac{1}{2}\). Matches option B.
note: follows the corrected stem nCr/32 (paper: (ans).md Q129 'nC0+...+nCn over 32 = 1, 2^n = 32, n = 5'); the stored sum used the misprinted (3/2)^n
the stored 874/90^4 is wrong: (22016+256)/90^4 = 22272/90^4 = 87(4/90)^4 (paper's key solution); the corrected option C is 87(4/90)^4

solution: p(can't solve) = 4/7, q(can solve) = 3/7. \(P(X\leq 2) = P(0)+P(1)+P(2)\), \(n=20\). Each term has the factor \(\left(\frac{4}{7}\right)^{18}\): \(P=\left(\frac{4}{7}\right)^{18}\cdot\frac{16+240+1710}{49}=\frac{1966}{49}\left(\frac{4}{7}\right)^{18}\). Matches option B.
note: 1966*49^4/7^18 is not the sum; P(0)+P(1)+P(2) = (4/7)^18 (16+240+1710)/49 (paper's key solution agrees) = 1966/49 (4/7)^18, option B as the paper prints it

solution: One step from the start means 6 forward and 5 backward, or 5 forward and 6 backward. \(P = {}^{11}C_6(0.4)^6(0.6)^5 + {}^{11}C_5(0.4)^5(0.6)^6 = {}^{11}C_6(0.4)^5(0.6)^5(0.4+0.6) = {}^{11}C_6(0.24)^5\). Answer key gives (b) \({}^{11}C_6(0.24)^5\). Matches option B.
note: the stored working counted one direction only and reached option C; 'one step away' is either side (paper's key solution adds both, = 11C6(0.24)^5, key B)

solution: Using \(\sin2x = 2\tan x/(1+\tan^2x)\) and substituting \(t=\tan x\), integral reduces to \(\frac{1}{2}\int_{1/\sqrt{3}}^1\frac{t^4}{t^{10}+1}dt\). Further substituting \(u=t^5\) gives \(\frac{1}{10}\int_{1/(9\sqrt{3})}^1\frac{du}{1+u^2}=\frac{1}{10}\left[\frac{\pi}{4} - \tan^{-1}\frac{1}{9\sqrt{3}}\right]\). Matches option C.
note: t = tan x (not tan^5 x) gives (1/2) int t^4/(t^10+1) dt; u = t^5 gives (1/10) int_{1/(9 sqrt3)}^1 du/(1+u^2); (1/sqrt3)^5 = 1/(9 sqrt3); key C

solution: Substitute \(x = \cos\theta\): integral becomes \(\int_0^{\pi/2} \tan\frac{\theta}{2}\sin\theta\,d\theta\). Since \(\tan\frac{\theta}{2}\sin\theta = 2\sin^2\frac{\theta}{2} = 1-\cos\theta\), the integral is \(\int_0^{\pi/2}(1-\cos\theta)\,d\theta = \frac{\pi}{2} - 1\). Alternatively, rationalize and use standard results. Common mistake: missing the constant term after integration.
note: the simplification and the integral were not shown; added (tan(t/2) sin t = 2 sin^2(t/2) = 1 - cos t)

solution: Rewrite as \(\int\frac{\sec^2 x}{\tan^{4/3}x}dx\); substitute \(t=\tan x\) to get \(\int t^{-4/3}dt=-3t^{-1/3}\Big|_{1/\sqrt3}^{\sqrt3}\). Evaluating gives \(3^{7/6}-3^{5/6}\). Matches option B.
note: t-limits: tan(pi/6)=1/sqrt3 and tan(pi/3)=sqrt3 (the x-limits were kept on a t-antiderivative)

solution: \(x = 0, y = 0, z = 1\) gives \(1, 7, 2\) in the three equations; the determinant is \(13 \ne 0\), so this is the only solution.

If \(B=A^{-1}\) then \(AB=I\). Row 1 of \(A\) times column 1 of \(B\): \(-2+7+c=1\Rightarrow c=-4\); row 1 times column 3: \(b-2+1=0\Rightarrow b=1\); row 2 times column 1: \(-2+7a+3c=0\Rightarrow7a=14\Rightarrow a=2\). Then \(4a+2b-c=8+2+4=14\). Check: row 2 times column 2 gives \(-a+3=1\) for \(a=2\), as \(AB=I\) requires.
note: the remark that row 2 x column 2 gives 1 != 0 was wrong: AB=I needs that entry to be 1, and -a+3=1 for a=2; B is A^-1 and the stem has no defect

solution: \(\frac{dp}{dt} = kp \Rightarrow p = p_0 e^{kt}\). At \(t=40\): \(80 = 40e^{40k}\), so \(e^{40k}=2\). At \(t=80\): \(p = 40 \times e^{80k} = 40 \times 4 = 160\) thousand \(= 160000\). Matches option C: 160000.
note: 40 is in thousands: 40 x 4 = 160 thousand = 160000

solution: Dividing by \(x^2y^2\) and regrouping: \(d\!\left(-\frac{1}{xy}\right)+d(\log x)-d(\log y)=0\Rightarrow\log\frac{x}{y}=\frac{1}{xy}+k\). Matches option B.
note: d(log x)-d(log y) integrates to log(x/y), not log(xy)

solution: Newton's law: \(\frac{T-T_0}{T_1-T_0}=e^{-kt}\). After 30 min: \(\frac{60-30}{80-30}=e^{-30k}\Rightarrow e^{-30k}=3/5\). After 60 min: \(T-30 = 50\cdot(3/5)^2=18\), \(T=48^{\circ}C\). Matches option C.
note: denominator T_1 - T_0 (T_0 = 30 room, T_1 = 80), matching the next line (60-30)/(80-30)

solution: Family: \(x^2+y^2=2bx\). Differentiating and eliminating b: \((x^2+y^2)^2=4x^2\!\left(x+y\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2\). Matches option A.
note: stray trailing x^2 removed: (x^2+y^2)^2 = 4x^2 (x + y y')^2

solution: Dividing by \(x\log x\): IF \(= e^{\int\frac{1}{x\log x}dx} = \log x\). Solution: \(y\log x = 2(x\log x - x)+c\). At \(x=1\), \(y\log x=0\): \(0=2(0-1)+c\Rightarrow c=2\). At \(x=e\): \(y(e) = 0+2 = 2\). Matches option A.
note: y(1)=0 is not given by the stem: at x=1 the left side y log x is 0, so c=2; the value asked is y(e)

solution: Separate variables: \(\frac{y+1}{y}dy = -e^x(\cos^2x - \sin2x)dx\). Note \(-e^x(\cos^2x-\sin2x) = -\frac{d}{dx}[e^x\cos^2x]\). Integrating: \(y + \ln y = -e^x\cos^2x + C\). Apply \(y=1, x=0\): \(1+0 = -1+C\Rightarrow C=2\). Hence \(y+\ln y + e^x\cos^2x = 2\). Common mistake: not recognising the RHS as an exact derivative.
note: d/dx[e^x cos^2 x] = e^x(cos^2 x - sin 2x), so the RHS is MINUS that derivative: y+ln y = -e^x cos^2 x + C, C=2

solution: Using substitution \(y = vx\) gives \(\sec^2 v\, dv = -dx/x\). Integrating: \(\tan v = -\ln x + c\). Applying \((1, \pi/4)\): \(c=1\). So \(y = x\tan^{-1}\left(\ln\frac{e}{x}\right)\). Matches option C.
note: tan v = 1 - ln x = ln(e/x), so y = x tan^-1(ln(e/x)) (option C); 'ln ex' was a different expression

solution: \(C_3 e^{x+C_4} = C_3 e^{C_4} e^x = B e^x\). So \(y = (C_1 + C_2)e^x + B e^x = Ae^x\): only 1 arbitrary constant. Order = 1. Matches option B: 1.
note: (C1+C2)e^x + Be^x = Ae^x with A = C1+C2+B: one arbitrary constant, order 1

solution: Tangent to \(x^2=4y\) (here \(4a=4\), so \(a=1\)) in slope form: \(x=my+\dfrac{1}{m}\), i.e. \(mx=m^2y+1\). Replace \(m=\dfrac{dx}{dy}=\dfrac{1}{dy/dx}\): \(x\dfrac{dy}{dx}=y+\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^2\). This is order 1, degree 2.
note: m = dx/dy (the tangent x = my + 1/m has slope 1/m): mx = m^2 y + 1 gives x y' = y + y'^2

solution: Implicit differentiation w.r.t. \( y \). At \( (\pi/4,\pi/4) \): \( \cos x = \cos y = 1/\sqrt{2} \). After differentiation and substitution: \( \frac{dx}{dy} = \frac{(a+\sqrt{2}\,b\cos x)\sin y}{(a-\sqrt{2}\,b\cos y)\sin x} = \frac{(a+b)\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}{(a-b)\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}  \). Simplifies to \( \frac{a+b}{a-b} \). Matches option B.
note: dx/dy = (a + sqrt2 b cos x) sin y / ((a - sqrt2 b cos y) sin x) (stored had it inverted, with 2b); at pi/4 it is (a+b)/(a-b)

solution: \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{10(\sec^{10}\theta+\cos^{10}\theta)}{\sec\theta+\cos\theta}\). Since \(\sec\theta\cos\theta=1\), \(x^2+4=(\sec\theta+\cos\theta)^2\) and \(y^2+4=(\sec^{10}\theta+\cos^{10}\theta)^2\); squaring the result for \(dy/dx\) gives \((x^2+4)(dy/dx)^2 = 100(y^2+4)\), so \(k = 100\). Matches option D: 100.
note: the identity was not shown: x^2+4 and y^2+4 are perfect squares because sec*cos = 1

solution: Differentiating \(y^2=(x+c)^3\): \(2y\,dy/dx = 3(x+c)^2\). From \(2y\,y'=3(x+c)^2\): \((x+c)^2=\frac{2y\,y'}{3}\), so \((x+c)^3=y^2\) gives \(\left(\frac{2y\,y'}{3}\right)^{3/2}=y^2\); squaring, \(\frac{8y^3y'^3}{27}=y^4\), so \(8(dy/dx)^3 = 27y\). Matches option C.
note: the working broke off at \cdots; spelled out the elimination of c

solution: This is a Bernoulli equation in \(x(y)\). Put \(t=\frac{1}{x}\), so \(\frac{dt}{dy}=-\frac{1}{x^2}\frac{dx}{dy}\); dividing the equation by \(x^2\) gives \(\frac{dt}{dy}-\frac{t}{y}=-1\). The integrating factor is \(\frac{1}{y}\), so \(\frac{d}{dy}\left(\frac{t}{y}\right)=-\frac{1}{y}\), giving \(\frac{t}{y}=-\ln y+c\). So \(\frac{1}{x} = cy - y\ln y\). Matches option B.
note: worked solution for dx/dy + x/y = x^2 (the stem as printed in the paper)

solution: Highest order derivative is \(\frac{d^3y}{dx^3}\) (order \(m=3\)). Multiplying by \(\frac{d^3y}{dx^3}\) clears the fraction, and then \(\frac{d^3y}{dx^3}\) occurs to the power 2, so degree \(n=2\). \(m^2+n^2=9+4=13\). Matches option B: 13.
note: stored [1] said degree 1 but [2] used n=2; the stem (as the paper prints it) gives n=2 after clearing the fraction

solution: The continued fraction repeats, so \(y=\dfrac{\sin x}{1+\dfrac{\cos x}{1+y}}\), i.e. \(y(1+y+\cos x)=(1+y)\sin x\). Differentiating w.r.t. \(x\): \(y'(1+2y+\cos x-\sin x)=y\sin x+(1+y)\cos x\), which gives option A. Matches option A.
note: stored [0] y(1+cos x - sin x) = sin x (1+y) is wrong (y(1+y+cos x) = (1+y) sin x); the differentiation is now shown

solution: Write \(\sin^{11/3}x\cos^{1/3}x=\tan^{11/3}x\cos^{4}x\), so the integrand is \(\tan^{-11/3}x\,(1+\tan^{2}x)\sec^{2}x\); substitute \(t = \tan x\). After integration: \(\int t^{-11/3}(1+t^{2})\,dt = -\frac{3}{8}t^{-8/3} - \frac{3}{2}t^{-2/3} = -\left(\frac{3}{8}\tan^{-8/3}x + \frac{3}{2}\tan^{-2/3}x\right)\). So \(f(x)=\tan^{-8/3}x\), \(g(x)=\tan^{-2/3}x\). Matches option A.
note: stem is the cube root of sin^11 x cos x with a minus outside the bracket; solution now derives the t-integral and the sign

solution: Substituting \(2x-1 = t^2\): after integration, \(= \frac{\sqrt{2x-1}\,(x+4)}{3} + c = \frac{(x+4)}{3}\sqrt{2x-1} + c\). Thus \(f(x) = \frac{x+4}{3}\). Matches option B: \(\frac{1}{3}(x+4)\).
note: the integral's value lacked its square root, so the two sides were not equal

solution: Divide numerator and denominator by \( \cos^{2}x \); let \( t = \tan x \). Integral becomes \( \int\frac{dx}{1+3\sin^{2}x} = \int\frac{\sec^{2}x\,dx}{1+4\tan^{2}x} = \int\frac{dt}{1+4t^{2}} \). \( \frac{1}{4}\int\frac{dt}{t^{2}+(1/2)^{2}} = \frac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}(2t) + c \), so \( f(x) = 2\tan x \). Matches option A.
note: dividing by cos^2 x gives sec^2 x/(1+4 tan^2 x), not the stored (1+t^2)+3t^2/(1+t^2) form; the arctan step is now shown

solution: Let \( t = \sec x \), \( dt = \sec x\tan x\,dx \). Integral \( = \int\frac{dt}{9-16(t^{2}-1)} = \int\frac{dt}{25-16t^{2}} = \frac{1}{40}\log\left|\frac{5+4t}{5-4t}\right|+c \). Matches option B.
note: the paper has no square root; with sqrt the 1/40 log form would not follow

solution: Substituting \(\log x=t\): integral becomes \(\frac{1}{2}\int(\sec^2\frac{t}{2}+2\tan\frac{t}{2})e^t\,dt=\tan\frac{t}{2}\cdot e^t+C=x\tan\frac{\log x}{2}+C\). Matches option D.
note: sec^2 printed without its backslash

solution: Let \(t = 3^{x/2}\); as \(x\to 2\), \(t\to 3\). Numerator \(\to t^2+27/t^2-12\), denominator \(\to 27/t^2-t\). Both tend to \(0\) as \(t\to3\); by L'Hôpital in \(t\): numerator \(\to 2t-54/t^{3} = 4\), denominator \(\to -54/t^{3}-1 = -3\), so the limit is \(-4/3\). Matches option A: \(-4/3\).
note: the limit was stated, not derived; the derivatives in t are now worked

solution: Rationalise numerator and denominator; at \(x=a\): \(\lim = \frac{(a+2x)-(3x)}{(3a+x)-(4x)}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{3a+x}+2\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{a+2x}+\sqrt{3x}} = \frac{a-x}{3(a-x)}\cdot\frac{4\sqrt{a}}{2\sqrt{3}\sqrt{a}}=\frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}=\frac{2}{3\sqrt{3}}\). Matches option C.
note: at x=a the second factor is 4 sqrt(a)/(2 sqrt3 sqrt a)=2/sqrt3; the stored 3sqrt a/(2 sqrt a) and 1/(2 sqrt3) = 2/(3 sqrt3)/1 were wrong

solution: RHL: rationalise to get \(\lim_{x\to0^+}\frac{\sqrt{x}(\sqrt{16+\sqrt{x}}+4)}{\sqrt{x}} \to 8\). LHL: \(\frac{k^2}{2}\). For continuity: \(k^2/2 = 8 \Rightarrow k = 4\). Matches option A.
note: after rationalising, (16+sqrt x)-16 = sqrt x, so the denominator is sqrt x, not x

solution: Rationalising twice: limit reduces to \(\frac{1}{(\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{2})(1+1)} = \frac{1}{4\sqrt{2}}\). Matches option C.
note: the extra 1 in the first factor made the product 2(1+2 sqrt2), not 4 sqrt2

solution: Factor denominator: \(x^3-3x^2+2x = x(x-1)(x-2)\). Combine fractions: \(\frac{x(x-1)-2}{x(x-1)(x-2)} = \frac{x^2-x-2}{x(x-1)(x-2)} = \frac{(x-2)(x+1)}{x(x-1)(x-2)}\). Cancel \((x-2)\) and take limit: \(\frac{3}{2\times1} = \frac{3}{2}\). Matches option C: \(\frac{3}{2}\).
note: the numerator of the second fraction is 2, not 2x; x^2-x-2 = (x-2)(x+1) then follows

solution: Substituting \( t = \pi/2-x \to 0 \): numerator: \( \frac{1-\tan(x/2)}{1+\tan(x/2)}=\tan\frac{t}{2}\sim\frac{t}{2} \) and \( 1-\sin x=1-\cos t\sim\frac{t^2}{2} \), so \( \sim\frac{t}{2}\cdot\frac{t^2}{2}=\frac{t^3}{4} \); denominator \( \sim 8t^3 \). The limit is \( \frac{t^3/4}{8t^3} = \frac{1}{32} \). Matches option B: \( 1/32 \).
note: numerator is ~ t^3/4 (not t^4 order); with denominator 8t^3 the limit is 1/32, now shown

solution: As \(x\to0^-\), \([x]=-1\) and \(|x|=-x\). Expression: \(\frac{x(-1+(-x))\sin(-1)}{-x}=\frac{x(-1-x)(-\sin1)}{-x}=-(-1-x)(-\sin1)\to-(-1)(-\sin1)=-\sin1\). Matches option D.
note: the factor x/(-x) = -1 was dropped, so (-1)(-sin1) = +sin1 did not equal the stated -sin1

solution: \(\lim_{x\to 0}(1+\tan x)^{\csc x}/(1+\sin x)^{\csc x}\). The base \(\to 1\) while \(\csc x\to\infty\), a \(1^\infty\) form, so \(\lim = e^{\lim \csc x\,(\text{base}-1)}\) with \(\text{base}-1=\frac{\tan x-\sin x}{1+\sin x}\). Formal: \(\lim = e^{\lim \frac{\csc x(\tan x - \sin x)}{1+\sin x}} = e^{\lim \frac{1/\cos x - 1}{1+\sin x}} = e^0 = 1\). Matches option B: 1.
note: (1+0)/(1+0)=1 is invalid for a 1^infinity form; replaced by the exponent route, with the missing 1/(1+sin x) factor restored

solution: Write \(\left(\frac{x+2}{x+4}\right)^2 = \frac{x^2+4x+4}{(x+4)^2} = \frac{x(x+4)}{(x+4)^2} + \frac{4}{(x+4)^2} = \frac{x}{x+4} + \frac{4}{(x+4)^2}\). With \(f(x) = \frac{x}{x+4}\): \(f'(x) = \frac{4}{(x+4)^2}\), so the integrand is \(e^x[f(x)+f'(x)]\) and \(\int e^x[f(x)+f'(x)]dx = e^x f(x) + c\). Matches option A: \(\frac{e^x x}{x+4}+c\).
note: solution followed a misread stem (x+2)/(x+4)^2 and its own check failed; rewritten for the paper's ((x+2)/(x+4))^2 (the paper's key working)

solution: Using \(\sin x+\sin^3x=\sin x(1+\sin^2x)\) and \(\cos 2x=1-2\sin^2x\); substituting \(\cos x=t\) gives \(I=\int\frac{t^2-2}{2t^2-1}dt=\frac{1}{2}\int dt-\frac{3}{2}\int\frac{dt}{2t^2-1}=\frac{1}{2}t-\frac{3}{4\sqrt{2}}\log\left|\frac{\sqrt{2}t-1}{\sqrt{2}t+1}\right|+C\), so \(P=\frac{1}{2}\) and \(Q=-\frac{3}{4\sqrt{2}}\). Matches option B.
note: working only stated P and Q; the integral is now worked (t = cos x), for the paper's log argument (sqrt2 cos x -1)/(sqrt2 cos x +1)

solution: \(\left[\frac{x}{2}\right]\) jumps by \(1\) at every even integer, so \(f(x)=x\left[\frac{x}{2}\right]\) can be discontinuous only there. At \(x=0\) the jump is multiplied by \(x=0\), so \(f\) is continuous there. At \(x=\pm2,\pm4,\pm6,\pm8\) the jump is \(x\neq0\), so \(f\) is discontinuous at these \(8\) points of \((-10,10)\). Matches option D.
note: solution followed the wrong stem [x[x/2]] and listed -4..4; rewritten for x[x/2]

solution:
With \(x=\sin t,\ y=\sin pt\): \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{p\sqrt{1-y^2}}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\).
Writing \(\sqrt{1-x^2}\,y'=p\cos pt\) and differentiating again: \(\sqrt{1-x^2}\,y''-\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\,y'=-\dfrac{p^2\sin pt}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\), so \((1-x^2)y''-xy'=-p^2y\) and \((1-x^2)y''-xy'+p^2y=0\).
note: the stored line states the result of the second differentiation without doing it; the paper differentiates dy/dx = p cos pt / cos t again

solution: Put \(x=\tan\theta\) in \(y=\tan^{-1}\!\dfrac{\sqrt{1+x^2}-1}x=\dfrac\theta2\Rightarrow\dfrac{dy}{d\theta}=\dfrac12\). Put \(x=\sin\theta\) in \(z=\tan^{-1}\!\dfrac{2x\sqrt{1-x^2}}{1-2x^2}=2\theta\Rightarrow\dfrac{dz}{d\theta}=2\). Here \(\theta=\tan^{-1}x\) in the first and \(\theta=\sin^{-1}x\) in the second, so \(y=\tfrac12\tan^{-1}x\) and \(z=2\sin^{-1}x\): \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{1}{2(1+x^2)}\), \(\dfrac{dz}{dx}=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\), and at \(x=0\) \(\dfrac{dy}{dz}=\dfrac{1/2}{2}=\dfrac14\).
note: dy/dtheta / dz/dtheta is not dy/dz (different theta in the two substitutions) and the ratio is not independent of x; at x=0 it is 1/4

solution: Differentiating implicitly: \(\dfrac{1+y'}{x+y}=2xy'+2y\); at \(x=0\), \(\log y=0\) so \(y=1\), and \(\dfrac{1+y'}{1}=2\), so \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=1\). Matches option A: 1.
note: the working stated the result without the differentiated equation or its value at (0, 1)

solution: Rewrite \(y = \frac{\log\tan x}{\log\sin x}\). Using quotient rule and evaluating at \(x = \pi/4\): the numerator is \(2\log\sin\frac{\pi}{4} - 0 = -\log 2\) (the second term vanishes since \(\log\tan(\pi/4) = 0\)) and the denominator is \(\left(\log\sin\frac{\pi}{4}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{4}\log^2 2\). Result = \(\dfrac{-\log 2}{\frac{1}{4}\log^2 2} = -\dfrac{4}{\log 2}\). Matches option C: \(-\dfrac{4}{\log 2}\).
note: the value is -4/log 2 (the paper's own working), not -4 log 2; follows the option copy fix

solution: Write \(\frac{6x\sqrt{x}}{1-9x^3} = \frac{2\cdot3x\sqrt{x}}{1-(3x\sqrt{x})^2}\). Let \(u=3x\sqrt{x}=3x^{3/2}\), so \(\tan^{-1}\) arg \(= \tan^{-1}(2u/(1-u^2)) = 2\tan^{-1}u\). Then \(\frac{d}{dx}[2\tan^{-1}(3x^{3/2})] = \frac{2}{1+9x^3}\cdot\frac{9}{2}\sqrt{x} = \frac{9\sqrt{x}}{1+9x^3}\) This is \(\sqrt{x}\cdot\frac{9}{1+9x^3}\). Hence \(g(x) = \frac{9}{1+9x^3}\). Matches option D.
note: the derivative 9 sqrt(x)/(1+9x^3) = sqrt(x)·g(x) (stem restored by the copy fix); the stored lines wrote x·g(x) and then divided by sqrt x
the step was left as '...' and the x terms that cancel were never shown (the paper shows tan^-1 4x - tan^-1 x)

solution: \(h(x) = e^{\sin^{-1}x}\). \(h'(x) = e^{\sin^{-1}x} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\). So \(\frac{h'(x)}{h(x)} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\) and \(\left(\frac{h'(x)}{h(x)}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{1-x^2}\). The required value is \(\frac{1}{1-x^2}\). Matches option C.
note: the stem asks (h'/h)^2 (copy fix); the stored lines worked h'/h^2 and then h'/h

solution: Differentiate implicitly: \(\frac{1+y'}{x+y}=2(xy'+y)\). At \(x=0\): \(\log y=0\Rightarrow y=1\). Substituting: \(\frac{1+y'}{1}=2(0\cdot y'+1)\Rightarrow y'=1\). Matches option C.
note: at x=0, y=1 the right side 2(xy'+y) is 2, not 2y'

solution: Simplify to get \(y=\frac{\pi}{2}-2\tan^{-1}(e^x)\), so \(y'=\frac{-2e^x}{1+e^{2x}}\). At \(t=\frac{1}{2}\), \(\tan\frac{y}{2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\), so \(e^x=\frac{1-\tan(y/2)}{1+\tan(y/2)}=\frac{\sqrt{3}-1}{\sqrt{3}+1}\); substituting gives \(y'=-\frac{1}{2}\). Matches option B.
note: y = pi/2 - 2 tan^-1(e^x) (the paper's own line); with the root restored tan(y/2) = 1/sqrt3 at t = 1/2, which gives e^x

solution: Let \(x = \cos\theta\). Then \(\tan^{-1}\sqrt{\dfrac{1-\cos\theta}{1+\cos\theta}} = \tan^{-1}\left(\tan\dfrac{\theta}{2}\right) = \theta/2 = \cos^{-1}x/2\). Also \(\cos^{-1}(4x^3-3x) = \cos^{-1}(\cos 3\theta) = 3\theta = 3\cos^{-1}x\). Ratio of derivatives \(= (1/2)/(3) = 1/6\). Matches option D: \(\frac{1}{6}\).
note: the stored line drops the square root (and (1-cos)/(1+cos) = tan^2(theta/2), not tan(theta/2)); follows the stem copy fix

solution: Substituting \(\sin2x=\frac{2\tan x}{1+\tan^2x}\) and \(t=\tan x\): integral becomes \(\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{1+t^2}{\sqrt{t}}\,dt\), giving \(A=\frac{1}{2},B=\frac{5}{2},C=\frac{1}{5}\). \(5(A+B+C)=5\cdot\frac{16}{5}=16\). Matches option C: 16.
note: the integrand is (1+t^2)/(2 sqrt t); with 1/t the integral gives logs, not A=1/2, B=5/2, C=1/5

solution: \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\sec(\tan^{-1}x)\tan(\tan^{-1}x)\cdot\frac{1}{1+x^2}=\sqrt{1+x^2}\cdot\frac{x}{1+x^2}=\frac{x}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}\). At \(x=1\): \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\). Matches option C: \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\).
note: the stored derivative x/(1+x^2) and value 1/2 are wrong (sec(tan^-1 x) = sqrt(1+x^2)); the note about duplicate options B and C is dropped because the copy fix removes the duplicate

solution: Rewrite each term using \(\tan^{-1}A-\tan^{-1}B\) and \(\tan^{-1}A+\tan^{-1}B\) formulas. \(\dfrac{\log(e/x^2)}{\log(ex^2)}=\dfrac{1-2\log x}{1+2\log x}\), so the first term is \(\tan^{-1}1-\tan^{-1}(2\log x)=\dfrac{\pi}{4}-\tan^{-1}(2\log x)\). The second term is \(\tan^{-1}\dfrac{4+2\log x}{1-(4)(2\log x)}=\tan^{-1}4+\tan^{-1}(2\log x)\). The expression simplifies to a constant, \(y=\dfrac{\pi}{4}+\tan^{-1}4\); hence \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0\). Matches option A.
note: the rewrites were not shown; added them (key unchanged)

solution: Substituting \(t = \tan x\): integrand becomes \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\int(t^{-1/2} + t^{3/2})dt = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(2\sqrt{t}+\frac{2}{5}t^{5/2}\right)\); simplification gives \(\sqrt{2}\left(\sqrt{\tan x} + \frac{1}{5}(\tan x)^{5/2}\right) + c\). Matches option A.
note: the stored constant 1/2 should be 1/sqrt2 (since sqrt(2 sin x cos x) leaves (1+t^2)/sqrt(2t)) and the result is sqrt2(...); the '· ...' stub is replaced by the integrated terms

solution: Since \(2+\cos\frac{x}{2}=2\left(1+\frac{1}{2}\cos\frac{x}{2}\right)\) and \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(x+\sin\frac{x}{2}\right)=1+\frac{1}{2}\cos\frac{x}{2}\), the integrand is \(2\cdot\frac{(x+\sin(x/2))'}{x+\sin(x/2)}\). So the integral is \(2\log\left|x+\sin\frac{x}{2}\right|+C\). Matches option A.
note: the stored working belonged to a different integrand ((2+cos x)/(2x+sin x)^2) and ended on a different result; rewritten for the paper's integrand

solution: Using substitution \(1-x=t^2\): \(x = 1-t^2\), \(dx=-2t\,dt\), integral becomes \(-2\int(1-t^2)^2\,dt\). After expanding and integrating, \(-2\left(t-\frac{2t^3}{3}+\frac{t^5}{5}\right)=\sqrt{1-x}\left[-2+\frac{4(1-x)}{3}-\frac{2(1-x)^2}{5}\right]=-\frac{2}{15}\sqrt{1-x}\,(3x^2+4x+8)+c\), so \(p = -\frac{2}{15}\). Matches option A.
note: the stored integral -2 int (1-t^2)^2 t^2 dt has an extra t^2 (the stem has sqrt in the denominator, restored by the copy fix); the expansion is now shown

solution: Let \(t = \tan\sqrt{x}\), so \(dt = \frac{\sec^2\sqrt{x}}{2\sqrt{x}}\,dx\). The integral becomes \(2\int t^4\,dt = \frac{2}{5}t^5 + C = \frac{2}{5}\left[\tan\sqrt{x}\right]^5 + C\). Matches option C.
note: the stored working was abandoned ('Actually...', 1/sqrt x as a constant); with the stem restored the substitution t = tan sqrt x does it

solution: Write \(\frac{5\tan x}{\tan x-2}=\frac{5\sin x}{\sin x-2\cos x}\) and put \(5\sin x=A(\sin x-2\cos x)+B(\cos x+2\sin x)\), since \(\cos x+2\sin x\) is the derivative of \(\sin x-2\cos x\). Comparing coefficients: \(A+2B=5\) and \(-2A+B=0\), so \(A=1,\ B=2\). Hence the integral is \(x+2\log|\sin x-2\cos x|+c\), so \(a=2\). Matches option C.
note: the stored working named the method without doing it (and wrote B times sec^2 x times denom.); the coefficients are now shown
